item.title: Abuse Survivor Grace Nagamine Running for HD 51 Turns Zorro Ranch Failures Into a Plan to Protect New Mexicans
item.description:
Grace Nagamine, an Independent and survivor of sexual abuse and domestic violence, releases an eight-point agenda on sex-offender registration, survivors' filing deadlines, rape-kit testing and victim services.

ALAMOGORDO — Five days before Election Day, Independent House District 51 candidate Grace Nagamine released a policy brief that treats Jeffrey Epstein's Zorro Ranch not as a political scandal but as a lesson in how New Mexico fails survivors of sexual abuse — and what lawmakers should do about it.

The brief, titled "Lessons From Zorro Ranch: A Survivor's Plan to Protect New Mexicans From Sexual Abuse," lays out what Nagamine calls the Survivor Justice and Predator Accountability Agenda for the 2027 legislative session.

Its eight planks would make a predator's criminal history follow him into New Mexico, give childhood abuse survivors far more time to seek justice in court, force the state to test rape kits on time, tighten domestic violence protections, put permanent money behind survivor services, and build accountability that outlasts any one scandal.

The stakes are not limited to one ranch in Santa Fe County. According to the 2024 New Mexico Crime Victimization Report, cited in a 2026 Senate memorial, 54% of New Mexicans have experienced sexual assault or rape in their lifetimes. Advocates say about two-thirds of survivors never receive professional help.

"Zorro Ranch was allowed to happen because every institution assumed someone else would act," Nagamine said. "That's not only a story about a billionaire. It's how most abuse goes unpunished, here in Otero County too."

Nagamine, a lifelong Alamogordo resident, grandmother, founder of the humanitarian group Royal Angels and a former Mrs. New Mexico, says her own experience of sexual abuse and domestic violence is why the issue is personal rather than political.

"Survivors know what it is to carry abuse in silence, to wonder if anyone will believe you, and to find out the law says you waited too long," “unlike my competitor I have a unique perspective of survival,” she said. "I'll judge every vote by one question: does this help a survivor be believed, be safe, and get justice?"

Grace spoke of survival of childhood sexual abuse at a recent survivors rally spotlighting the needs of domestic abuse and sexual abuse victims: 

That perspective shows in the brief's details. It calls for survivors' names and identifying information to be redacted from any investigative files the state releases, for sexual assault nurse examiners within reach of rural towns such as Tularosa and Cloudcroft, and for quarterly county-by-county data on rape-kit testing so survivors can see whether their evidence is moving.

She also ties sexual violence to domestic violence, calling for full enforcement of protective orders and New Mexico's law requiring people under domestic violence protective orders to surrender firearms, plus lethality screening to flag the most dangerous cases early.

Running as an Independent, Nagamine argues that survivors are poorly served by party fights. "Survivors don't have a party, and neither do the people who failed them," she said. "I'll hold Democrats and Republicans to the same standard."

Nagamine's brief pairs every proposal with a failure it is meant to fix. Taken together, the eight reforms reach well beyond Zorro Ranch to the everyday cases that never make headlines.

1. Make a predator's history follow him. Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida in 2008 to a sex offense involving a minor, yet he was never registered as a sex offender in New Mexico, where he owned a 7,600-acre ranch. Nagamine wants a full update of the state's Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act to meet federal standards, building on a 2026 bill, HB 199, that covers offenders who move, work or study here. She would go further, requiring registration for anyone with a sex-offense conviction who owns or regularly stays at property in New Mexico, and funding the Department of Public Safety to clear its backlog of out-of-state conviction reviews. She also wants fingerprint-based background and registry checks for anyone working or volunteering with children, including private camps, ranches and residential programs.

"A predator's record shouldn't stop at the state line," Nagamine said. "If you have a conviction for abusing a child, New Mexico should know who you are the day you buy property here, not decades later."

2. Justice without an expiration date. Under current law, survivors of childhood sexual abuse generally must sue by age 24, or within three years of first disclosing the abuse to a licensed provider. Sponsors of reform legislation have told lawmakers survivors often do not come forward until their 50s. Nagamine would revive HB 151, which the House let die in committee in February, giving survivors far more time to file and reopening expired claims for three years. She would also review criminal limitations on sex crimes against children.

"Children don't get to choose when they're strong enough to speak," she said. "The law shouldn't punish them for how long it took."

3. Test every rape kit, on time. New Mexico once had the nation's worst per-capita backlog of untested sexual assault kits. After nearly a decade and more than $6 million spent, prosecutors warned lawmakers in 2025 that a new backlog was forming, with 134 kits at the state lab past the 180-day testing deadline set in 2019 and cases being delayed or dismissed. Nagamine would fund crime-lab staffing statewide, adopt the recommendations of a 2026 legislative task force on the backlog, and publish quarterly county-by-county testing data.

"An untested kit tells a survivor they don't matter," she said. "Every survivor in Otero County deserves to know where their evidence is."

4. No more deferring to nobody. In 2019, New Mexico's then-attorney general stepped aside for federal prosecutors in New York, shared the state's files and received nothing in return. The case died. Nagamine would require a written agreement guaranteeing the state copies of evidence and regular updates any time it pauses an investigation for another agency, with automatic reopening if that cooperation stops. She also backs Attorney General Raúl Torrez's lawsuit seeking unredacted federal files on Zorro Ranch.

5. Break the link between domestic violence and sexual abuse. Drawing on her own experience, Nagamine argues the two forms of violence often share the same abusers and the same silence. She calls for full funding to enforce protective orders and the state law requiring people under domestic violence protective orders to surrender their firearms, lethality-assessment screening so police and advocates can identify the most dangerous cases early, and more shelter, legal help and safety planning in rural counties.

"Domestic violence taught me that the most dangerous moment is often when you try to leave," she said. "Our laws have to be ready for that moment."

6. Fund the front lines. Federal Victims of Crime Act funding has been cut by roughly 40% since 2022, and 41 sexual assault provider organizations have been surviving on one-time state grants. Nagamine would make $2 million a year in sexual assault service funding permanent and guarantee access to a sexual assault nurse examiner near every community, including Alamogordo, Tularosa and Cloudcroft. Nearly 6,000 survivors used these services statewide last year; almost a third were children.

7. Protect survivors' privacy and dignity. Any investigative files the state releases should redact survivors' names and identifying details and exclude abuse imagery, the brief says. Nagamine would also strengthen the state's 2019 Sexual Assault Survivor's Bill of Rights with clear notice requirements, enforcement and a way to report violations.

8. Make accountability permanent. The House's Epstein Truth Commission has been weakened by disputes over an edited report and members' outside jobs, and is down to three of four members. If its work continues, Nagamine would re-create it in law as a joint House-Senate body with equal partisan membership, a 30-day deadline to fill vacancies, and a rule that every change to an official report be approved by all members and published. She would also require banks operating in New Mexico to train staff to spot and report signs of human trafficking.

"None of this is about one ranch or one billionaire," Nagamine said. "It's about every child and every woman in this state who was told to stay quiet. I was one of them. I'm not quiet anymore."

Epstein owned the ranch near Stanley from 1993 until his death in 2019. A legislative Survivors' Truth Commission reported in August that evidence supports abuse of at least five women and girls there, and that at least 30 more people may have been abused in New Mexico. No agency searched the property until March 2026.

Nagamine is challenging Republican Rep. John Block, who has represented District 51 since 2023. Block voted with the unanimous House in February to create the Truth Commission and called Zorro Ranch a "stain" on New Mexico during floor debate, according to the Albuquerque Journal.

After the commission's interim report came out in August, Block dismissed it in social media posts as "feeble" and a "nothing-burger" that "helps no victims," and said the money spent had gone "into the paper shredder."Nagamine says the difference is what comes after the criticism.

A review of Block's legislative record found no bill to extend survivors' filing deadlines, upgrade sex-offender registration or fund survivor services.

"Calling an investigation a nothing-burger is easy. It scores a point and helps no one," Nagamine said. "Survivors have heard enough politicians turn their pain into a partisan fight. A legislator's job is to write the laws that keep the next child safe. That's what I'll do."

The Truth Commission's final report is due in December, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez's criminal investigation and his Oct. 21 lawsuit against Epstein's lawyer and accountant, who deny the allegations, are ongoing. Nagamine says she would use the commission's findings as a starting point for legislation in the 60-day session that begins in January.

"The report shouldn't be the end of this," she said. "It should be the first draft of better laws."

Read the full policy brief, with sources: Lessons From Zorro Ranch: A Survivor's Plan to Protect New Mexicans From Sexual Abuse. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Survivors seeking support can reach the New Mexico Sexual Assault Helpline at 1-844-667-2457 or nmsahelp.org.

item.title: Commentary: Vote No on the County LEDA Tax: Show Us the Plan, the Books, and Who Gets Paid
item.description:
Alamogordo Editorial- On Tuesday, Otero County voters will decide whether to add a one-eighth-of-one-percent Local Economic Development Act (LEDA) gross receipts tax to nearly everything bought and sold in the county. Supporters describe it as a penny on an $8 purchase.

The real question is not the size of the penny.

It is whether this county government has earned the right to collect it, whether anyone has a plan to spend it, and who stands to benefit when it is spent.

On all three counts, the answer today is no

Voters should reject this measure and invite the county to come back when it can answer those questions in public.

Former Alamogordo city manager Stephanie Hernandez, an economist who has run LEDA-funded projects herself, put it plainly in a recent radio segment: "If this tax passes, what's the plan?" She noted that revenue from an eighth-cent tax will take years to accumulate before it can fund anything large, and that funding without a strategy is "just a wish."

She is right, and the county has not answered her. There is no published list of target industries, no site-readiness inventory, no pipeline of prospects, and no estimate of how many jobs per dollar the county expects. Voters are being asked to approve the revenue first and trust that a plan will follow. That is backwards.

Other community leaders are making the same point. Responding to an online explainer of what LEDA allows under state law, former Alamogordo Mayor Susan Payne wrote that state law "provides a framework, not a strategy" for Otero County, and that local governments have the flexibility to tailor LEDA to their own communities for exactly that reason. Her concern, she stressed, is not with LEDA itself or with the county's wish to pursue economic development. It is with asking residents, "many of whom are already struggling financially," to support another tax without a clearly defined local strategy, measurable goals, and a plan for achieving results.

Payne's conclusion is the right one: "Economic development should drive the need for funding, not the other way around. We need a strategy first, then determine how to fund it."

The strongest argument against handing Otero County a new revenue stream is the county's own audit.

The independent audit for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025, by Hinkle + Landers, identified six findings, three of them repeats from prior years, including several material weaknesses in internal control. Among them:

Capital assets: tracking and depreciation errors required more than $3.3 million in adjustments. This is a repeat finding first flagged in 2023.

Cash reconciliations: June 2025 bank reconciliations were off by $1.37 million.

Investments: cash and investments were commingled without fund-level separation, another repeat finding.

Federal grants: on the Operation Stonegarden program, all seven tested financial reports were filed late and six did not match the ledger; only seven of 24 required subrecipient reports were collected. Auditors issued a qualified opinion on the program.

Uncollateralized deposits: county deposits exceeded pledged collateral by $1.5 million, a violation of state law, and also a repeat.

LEDA's promised safeguards are project participation agreements and clawback provisions. Clawbacks only work if someone tracks performance, documents shortfalls, and actually goes after the money. A county that auditors say cannot consistently reconcile its bank accounts or collect required reports from its own federal subrecipients is not positioned to police complex, multi-year incentive contracts with private businesses.

The county's FY26 budget projected roughly $65.5 million in revenue against about $84.9 million in spending. It has paid more than $2 million to settle a wrongful-death suit over a 2023 suicide at the county detention center. It has lost expected dispatch revenue after Alamogordo left the regional dispatch authority. And this spring commissioners called a 12-minute emergency session to extend the ICE contract at the Otero County Processing Center, because that facility is the only source of revenue to repay the bonds that built it.

A government under that much fiscal pressure will feel enormous temptation to treat a new "dedicated" fund as a cushion. LEDA money cannot legally pay for road graders or lawsuit settlements, but it can be steered toward whatever projects are politically convenient, and it can sit idle while the county figures out what to do with it.

This is not the first time the commission has reached for gross receipts revenue. In August 2023, the commission voted 2–1 to impose a one-eighth-cent GRT increase without putting it on the ballot at all. Commissioner Amy Barela, the lone no vote, argued that voters should decide.

In 2022, the State Auditor sent the county a letter citing potential violations of county and state procurement code over its contract with EchoMail for an audit of the 2020 election, and questioned whether the commission had treated its office as a public trust. A separate state audit of county finances grew out of a commissioner's improperly approved travel voucher.

These episodes are not about economic development. They are about whether this county follows its own rules when spending public money. The track record says it often does not.

Alamogordo has run a LEDA program since 1996, and its history is a preview of what a county program could become:

The city sued the operator of the Fun Center bowling facility for breach of contract after the project, built with LEDA funds and public bond money, went sideways.

A proposed $1.9 million LEDA allocation drew public accusations of favoritism and of overriding staff recommendations, with residents asking how a dozen part-time jobs justified that much tax money.

In December 2025, the commission awarded $650,000 in LEDA money to upgrade bowling lanes at the city-owned Rocket City Family Fun Center, after the finance director reminded commissioners that LEDA funds can also be used for debt service and quality-of-life projects, not just job creation.

So much LEDA money piled up unspent that voters in 2024 rededicated the city's LEDA tax and at least $4 million of its fund balance to build an indoor pool. A pool may be a good investment, but it is not economic development, and it shows how a "dedicated" economic development tax drifts toward whatever a governing body wants once the balance grows large enough.

As recently as May 2026, roughly $900,000 to $1 million in remaining city LEDA funds sat on the table while commissioners argued over whether to spend it on demolishing derelict buildings.

If the city, with an experienced economic development staff, struggled to deploy LEDA money cleanly, there is little reason to expect better from a county whose auditors keep flagging basic control failures.

The state model ballot question the county is using makes retail businesses, cultural facilities, and arts and cultural districts qualifying uses. That is a wide door. It means LEDA dollars can subsidize a retailer that competes directly with existing local businesses that never asked for a handout, and those existing businesses will be the ones collecting and remitting the tax. Gross receipts taxes fall on services and labor as well as goods, and they hit lower-income households hardest because they spend a larger share of what they earn.

The Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce has posted what it calls a "public service announcement" about the measure. It describes the tax rate, lists qualifying uses, and highlights clawback safeguards and the 83 New Mexico communities with LEDA ordinances. It does not mention the county's audit findings, its budget gap, or any of the local LEDA controversies. A neutral voter guide would.

That matters because the Chamber is not a bystander.

In March 2026, the county attorney recommended that the commission authorize the Chamber as the lead organizer of a new Otero-Lincoln regional economic development initiative, handling day-to-day coordination and marketing. The Chamber's own website directs businesses considering relocation to contact the Chamber, and historically it shared office space and staff with the Otero County Economic Development Council, which makes recommendations to the city and county on LEDA-type incentives.

To be clear: no public evidence has surfaced of any agreement to pay the Chamber from LEDA revenue in exchange for its support, and this editorial does not allege one. But voters are entitled to know, before they vote, whether the organization promoting this tax expects to administer, market, or be paid from the money it raises.

That is a basic conflict-of-interest disclosure, and it costs nothing to make.

The Chamber and the commission should state publicly, in writing:

If the answers are "no, no, and a public board," say so.

Silence invites the very suspicion the Chamber would presumably like to avoid.

Voters are not against economic development. They are against writing blank checks. A proposal worth supporting would come with:

A published economic development plan naming target sectors and specific sites, adopted before any tax is collected.

A clean audit, or at minimum a resolved corrective action plan for the repeat findings.

A requirement that every project participation agreement, job commitment, and clawback action be posted online and reported annually.

A sunset clause, so the tax expires unless voters renew it after seeing results.

A written prohibition on using LEDA revenue to pay advocacy organizations or their members for administration or marketing.

None of that is in front of voters on Tuesday.

Economic development does not happen by accident, and it does not happen by tax increase alone. Otero County has not shown a plan, has not shown that it can manage the money it already collects, and has not answered reasonable questions about who will benefit. Until it does, the responsible vote is no.

item.title: Hallow’s Eve, Marvel’s Masked Halloween Antihero
item.description:
When I start to think about comic books during the Halloween season, I inevitably end up with one character in mind… Hallow’s Eve! She embodies the look and power set that most closely reminds me of the spooky season.

Sure, there are plenty of comic book characters inspired by myths, monsters, and supernatural forces. Few of those made Halloween masks their signature weapon. From her look to her power/skill set, Hallow’s Eve gives off the most Halloweenish vibes.

Elizabeth Tyne aka Janine Godbe aka Hallow’s Eve made her first appearance in Spider-man: The Lost Years #1 as the girlfriend of Ben Reilly. Every Spider-man fan should recognize the Ben Reilly name. If you don’t… Google it.

Hallow’s Eve has been labelled a villain and/or an anti-hero. Some readers even say she is just someone trying to reclaim control of her life. Honestly, I believe the character exists in the grey area between all three.

Hallow’s Eve was born Elizabeth Tyne. She killed her abusive father in self-defense. She panicked and went on the run and changed her name to Janine Godbe. While on the run, she met Ben Reilly and the two started a relationship.

It was during her relationship with Reilly that she encountered the Goblin Queen, Madelyne Pryor, the ruler of Limbo. Godbe tells Pryor about her insecurities and desire to support Reilly. Pryor uses S'ym's magic to empower Godbe, transforming her into Hallows' Eve. Godbe gained the ability to manifest masks with different abilities.

Who Is Janine Godbe?

Janine Godbe was born Elizabeth Tyne. Her father physically and sexually abused her all throughout her childhood. When she was 17 all those years of abuse finally pushed her to her breaking point. Tyne killed her father in self-defense.

Afraid of the consequences of killing her father, she panicked and went on the run. She changed her name to Janine Godbe and attempted to build a new life away from her past. Godbe struggled constantly with the fact she had killed someone, even if it was justified.

Ben Reilly was dealing with a different identity and issues in his past when he met Godbe. They were both living under assumed identities that concealed painful truths about their past. They both believed their past would make them unworthy of love. They were both damaged people who found acceptance in each other even though they struggled to accept themselves.

The Birth of Hallow’s Eve

During her time with Reilly, Godbe does what she can to support him. She allies with The Goblin Queen, Madelyn Pryor, ruler of Limbo. Godbe tells Pryor of her desire to support Reilly and her doubts of being able to so.

Pryor uses S’ym’s magic to transform her into Hallow’s Eve. Part of that transformation gave Godbe the ability to manifest masks with different abilities. She is also immune to Limbo based magic because of the transformation.

Godbe would later join the Blood Hunters, a supernatural crime fighting team. Their objective is to hunt down the vampires that remain after the vampire invasion. Their main antagonist is a superpowered vampire group called the Bloodcoven.

The Power of the Masks: Halloween with a Marvel Twist

Hallow’s Eve’s masks are enchanted and powered by chaos magic from Limbo. Each mask gives her a different ability, transformation, or disguise. She will be able to morph her powers and abilities according to which mask she is wearing. Oh, and she can change the masks mid-fight.

Some of the masks that have been revealed on the comic page are Frankenstein’s Monster (Strength & Power), Human Fly (Insect abilities, flight, acid projection), Werewolf (turns her into a werewolf), Ghost (invisibility & intangibility), Vampire (Supernatural abilities, flight, enhanced senses), Black Cat (Cat like creature with agility), Mummy (Mummy form where she can manipulate her wrappings), Witch (magical abilities), Captain America (Physical abilities, combat, shield), Hulk (tremendous strength and large physique), Spider-man (web-slinging, wall crawling), Wasp (flight, size manipulation, energy projection), Kaiju (transform into a large kaiju), Slasher (abilities of horror movie slasher), Police Officer (disguise as police officer), Model (disguise as a supermodel), and Gorilla (gorilla form with enhanced strength).

The problem with the masks being magically driven is everyone wants them. She is constantly targeted by those who want to steal the masks for themselves.

From Spider-Man Supporting Character to Solo Star

Godbe debuted in Spider-man: The Lost Years #1. She started off as Ben Reilly’s girlfriend, but she quickly became much more than that over the course of their relationship. Her first appearance as Hallow’s Eve was in Amazing Spider-man #14. This was part of the Dark Web crossover that helped establish her as a superpowered character rather than just Reilly’s girlfriend.

During the Dark Web events, Godbe helps the Goblin Queen in their campaign of revenge against Spider-man and the X-men. She joins other demons from Limbo in attacking New York. The attack ultimately fails, but it cements Godbe’s place as a force to be reckoned with in the Marvel universe.

Where Should New Readers Start?

If you are interested in catching up on this spooky themed character in time for Halloween, here is my suggested reading order:

Spider-man: The Lost Years #1 (1995) – Tyne/Godbe’s origin in Marvel Comics

Amazing Spider-man #14 (2022) – Godbe’s debut as Hallow’s Eve

Dark Web series (2022-2023) – Crossover that established Hallow’s Eve powers

Hallow’s Eve #1-5 (2023) – First solo miniseries

Hallow’s Eve: The Big Night (2023) – Follow up one shot

Conclusion

Hallow’s Eve is the perfect Halloween themed character. Her powers are derived from wearing magically enhanced masks. Those masks give her abilities associated with the subject of the mask. Putting on a mask and pretending to be someone/something else is the very essence of Halloween.

I would like to see Marvel bring Hallow’s Eve back into regular rotation. Even if she is just a minor character in a storyline. She would be great for a special Halloween season crossover series.

item.title: Former City Manager Hernandez on County LEDA Tax: “If This Tax Passes, What’s the Plan?”
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO N.M — With an Otero County economic development tax on the November ballot, former Alamogordo City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez used her weekly segment on KALH Radio this week to make a case that is neither for nor against the measure, but about what should come with it: a plan.

“I’m not here to tell anyone how to vote, but I do want to discuss its purpose,” Hernandez said in the commentary, part of her recurring “The Doctor Is In” segment with KALH host Anthony Lucero. “Economic development is a deliberate process.”

Statement on KALHRadio.org - The Dr is In

The county is asking voters to approve a separate one-eighth of one percent tax dedicated to economic development, a local option commonly tied to the state’s Local Economic Development Act, or LEDA. Hernandez, who holds degrees in economics and served as both assistant city manager and city manager for Alamogordo, said there is nothing wrong with wanting to bring industry to Otero County — but that wanting it is only the starting point.

“Vision without a strategy is just a wish,” she said. “We need to identify which industries fit our community, what they need to succeed, and what we’re able to invest in to attract the companies.”

Hernandez pointed to the city’s downtown as an example of the approach she is advocating. She said that as city manager she worked with the state, neighboring communities, business owners and local leadership to identify opportunities, and that economic development depends on collaboration, shared priorities and a common direction.

Downtowns, she said, function as economic hubs that support small businesses, tourism and private investment. When the city’s downtown effort began, she said, many buildings were vacant and dilapidated. “By the time I left, all the properties were rented and renovations underway,” she said. “That is progress and a win for Alamogordo.”

She said the same philosophy guided work on the zoo and the start of an economic plan for the airport and the industrial park: understand what the community has, invest in what it needs, and strategically pursue what it wants.

“Having funding available is one thing; having a plan to turn it into meaningful development is another.”

— Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, KALH Radio

Hernandez also revisited a financial decision from her time as assistant city manager, when the city faced a pool nearing the end of its useful life. The challenge, she said, was finding a solution without draining the city’s bonding capacity or raising taxes.

With her city manager’s support, she said, she brought an alternative to the City Commission, and voters ultimately approved reallocating the city’s existing LEDA tax and fund balance toward an indoor pool. Beyond meeting a community need, she said, a year-round aquatic facility could itself support economic development by hosting swim meets, attracting visitors and improving quality of life.

“That decision reflected our priorities, our limited resources, and the long-term needs,” she said.

Turning to the county proposal, Hernandez noted that if the tax is approved, revenues will take time to accumulate before they can fund larger investments. That lag, she argued, is exactly why the planning work — identifying opportunities, building partnerships and setting priorities — should begin now rather than after the money arrives.

She cautioned against viewing economic development as simply landing the next big employer. The work, she said, is about creating the conditions for growth: infrastructure, workforce development, support for existing businesses and building a community people want to live in.

“Economic development doesn’t happen by accident,” she said. “It takes vision and strategy.”

Her closing advice to voters was a single question: “If this tax passes, what’s the plan?”

Watch Dr. Hernandez’s full commentary, “The Doctor Is In — LEDA Tax,” on the KALH Radio YouTube channel: https://youtu.be/eVVv8IMU_hw

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez is a weekly commentator on KALHRadio.org. Commentary segments aired on KALH Radio reflect the views of the speaker.

item.title: Lady Bears Sweep Capitan as Otero County Volleyball Teams Struggle
item.description:
Otero County- Cloudcroft provided the lone bright spot for area volleyball this week, sweeping Capitan Thursday night while Alamogordo, Tularosa and Mescalero Apache all came up short.

The Lady Bears survived a marathon opening set, edging Capitan 30-28, then pulled away in the next two for a 25-22, 25-18 straight-set win. The victory lifts Cloudcroft to 11-8 overall and 3-2 in district play.

Cloudcroft returns home Saturday to host Lordsburg, then welcomes Mescalero Apache on Tuesday.

The Lady Tigers were swept by Organ Mountain earlier this week, 25-16, 25-13, 25-20. Alamogordo kept the third set close but couldn't force a fourth.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 6-14 overall and 0-6 in district. The Lady Tigers host Mayfield on Saturday.

Tularosa had a tough week, losing twice in two days.

In the first, Ruidoso beat the Lady Cats in four sets, 25-15, 18-25, 25-9, 25-14. Tularosa answered a lopsided first set by taking the second, but Ruidoso controlled the rest of the match.

Thursday at Dexter, the Lady Cats pushed every set but lost in three, 25-23, 25-20, 26-24. The third set went to extra points before Dexter closed it out.

Tularosa falls to 5-16 overall and 0-4 in district. The Lady Cats host NMMI on Tuesday.

Lordsburg rolled past the Lady Chiefs Thursday, 25-2, 25-6, 25-10. Mescalero Apache scored more in each successive set but couldn't slow Lordsburg.

The Lady Chiefs fall to 3-17 overall and 0-6 in district. They play at Cloudcroft on Tuesday.

Saturday, Oct. 31

Tuesday, Nov. 3

item.title: Endorsement: Alamogordo Needs a Leader Again at the Roundhouse, Grace Nagamine Is That Leader
item.description:
True Conservatives believe in results over rhetoric, accountability for public money, and leaders who answer to their neighbors rather than to political machines.

By those standards, the best choice in House District 51 this year is not the Republican on the ballot. It is independent, Grace Nagamine.

What real leadership looked like

Alamogordo doesn’t have to imagine what effective representation looks like. We once had it.

Ron Griggs served as our mayor, ran a local business, and then represented Otero County in the state Senate for more than a decade.

He was a Republican in a Democratic Legislature, and he still delivered:

• Wildfire prevention: In 2023, his bill banning prescribed burns on Red Flag warning days became law. Griggs credited the Legislature with passing it by unanimous, bipartisan vote.

• Economic development: He sponsored legislation lowering taxes on construction costs for large economic development projects, and legislation letting more small restaurants sell spirits.• Infrastructure: Local coverage noted his focus on job creation and his success securing capital funding for roads, public infrastructure, and other district projects.

Griggs never stopped being a conservative. He also never confused being loud with being effective. He built relationships across the aisle because that is how real dollars beyond standard outlays, and laws reach rural New Mexico.

Since his departure, that kind of true collaborative leadership has been missing from Alamogordo’s delegation.

Four years of a different approach

Rep. John Block has held the House District 51 seat since 2023. He moved here and flipped his alliances and recreated an identity taking advantage of local ideologies, (he interned for Martin Heinrich Democrat and worked for the Liberal Mayor Keller Campaign in Albuquerque while younger.) He has since whitewashed those facts and removed them from his public profiles. 

His defenders say a Republican can’t get anything done in a Democratic Legislature. Senator Griggs proved otherwise for years, and Block’s own colleagues prove it today:

• Other Republicans passed bills. In 2026, 25 of 26 House Republicans had a bill signed into law.

• He ranked near the bottom. Block ranked 19th of 26 by the share of his measures that passed.

• He led none of his signed bills. Three signed bills carry his name, and other legislators led all three.

• His own bills died early. All 33 measures he brought himself failed, most in their first committee.

His mailer claims more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County. That is the standard share of capital outlay every House member receives, added up over four years. Block chose his projects, then voted against the bills that funded them in 2023, 2025, and 2026.

In 2025 he also introduced a new 3.75% tax on renewable energy production. The free-market Southwest Public Policy Institute opposed it as harmful to consumers. That cost would have landed on PNM ratepayers, the same families who opened doubled and tripled PNM bills this year.

The difference is not ideology. Griggs and Block are both Republicans.

The difference is that one treated the Legislature as a place to build results for Alamogordo, and the other treats it as a stage for partisan fights.

Otero County has paid for that in lost opportunities.

Grace Nagamine: back to results

Grace Nagamine is a lifelong Alamogordo resident and a member of Mountain View Church for more than a decade. She survived homelessness and domestic violence, worked as a certified nursing assistant, cared for family, and founded Royal Angels to serve children with special needs.

Her platform is specific and in writing:

• Energy: She released a policy brief backing responsible oil and gas production and defending the permanent fund savings law.

• Holloman and veterans: She comes from an Air Force family and has made housing for military families a priority.

• Infrastructure: She has pledged to work with city leadership to bring state dollars to the roads, water lines, and sewer lines neglected for two decades.

• Transparency: She will publish every capital outlay request she makes.

• Partnership: She has committed to working with any legislator, Republican or Democrat, who will help Otero County, including regional partnership with District 33 state leadership and other leaders within the state

Grace Policy Statements:
https://graceforhd51.org/policy-statements/

Grace Platform and Policy Pillars:
https://graceforhd51.org/issues

That is the Griggs model: local roots, a plan, and the willingness to work with anyone to get it done.

Republicans, Democrats, and independents together

Nagamine’s support crosses party lines, the way a district representative’s should.

For those in the conservative community that are not convinced two Republicans who led Alamogordo City Hall are among those backing her.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, a Republican and former Alamogordo City Manager:

“I’m tired of divisive politics. New Mexico has fallen behind in too many areas, and I believe much of that comes from our inability to work together. Some of the deepest divisions aren’t even between political parties anymore. They’re within our own parties. We’ve become so focused on our differences that we’ve lost sight of the goals we share.

Somewhere along the way, we’ve confused fighting with leadership. Having served in local government, I know firsthand that progress requires relationships, cooperation, and the willingness to work with people who don’t always share your views. You can stand firm in your convictions without standing in the way of progress.

I know Grace Nagamine. She’s a fighter, but she also understands the value of teamwork. She knows the difference between fighting for people and simply fighting with people. Grace is willing to put differences aside, find common ground, and work toward what matters most: improving the lives of the people she represents. That’s why I’m supporting her.”

— Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, Republican, former Alamogordo City Manager

Susan Payne, a Republican and former Mayor of Alamogordo:

“For years, I’ve watched Santa Fe fail to address the issues that matter most to New Mexico families: our children’s education, their safety, and the growing concerns about crime in our communities.

As a former mayor, I know firsthand the consequences of failed policies. I had to lead our community through one of its darkest moments, the death of a police officer in the line of duty. It’s a tragedy that stays with you and one that strengthened my belief that our state must do better. Yet we continue to operate under a constitutional amendment that I believe has made it harder to hold dangerous criminals accountable and keep them off our streets.

Year after year, we hear the same promises, witness the same political division, and hope that something will finally change. But the issues remain, and our communities continue to pay the price.

That’s why I believe it’s time for a different approach. I believe Grace has what it takes to be a truly independent voice in Santa Fe. Someone who can work across party lines, find common ground, and put the needs of New Mexicans ahead of political agendas.

We cannot afford another year of the same excuses and the same results. Our state deserves leaders who recognize where we’ve fallen short and, more importantly, are willing to do something about it.

I’m supporting Grace because I believe it’s time to stop talking about change and start making it happen.”

— Susan Payne, Republican, former Mayor of Alamogordo

Republicans have joined Democrats and independents knocking on doors for her across the district.

They don’t agree on everything. But they agree Alamogordo deserves a representative who delivers - and are supportive of Grace Nagamine. With an army of over 100 individuals knocking on doors, dropping flyers and making phone calls she has support from grass roots neighbors not big corporations nor multiple major PACs. 

The fair objection

Some conservatives will say a vote for an independent weakens the Republican caucus, and that Block reliably votes the conservative line. 

But a reliable no vote is not the same as getting results for the local Alamogordo community. One House seat will not change which party controls the chamber

It will decide whether Alamogordo has an effective voice inside it.

Our endorsement

Alamogordo once had leaders who put this community ahead of party fights. It’s time to have one once again

Grace Nagamine is the voice Alamogordo needs now.

Early voting is underway, and Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Vote today.

This editorial was approved unanimously by the New Mexico Conservative News editorial advisory board, whose members include two Republicans, two Democrats, one Libertarian, and one member who declined to state a party.
